prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned body of prose and poetry in Romanian that turns memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: My first-round view holds on the criteria of voice, formal achievement and imaginative depth. Cărtărescu's prose is among the most recognizable on the shortlist. Public knowledge of the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid points to a single sustained project: a constructed interior cosmos built from memory, the body, the city and dream, carried by long, intricate syntax. His poetry from the 1980s onward belongs to the same project, so a citation can name poetry and prose together without stretching the scope. The oeuvre is long, developed over decades, and its late novels still look ambitious, which bears on sustained quality. The test I would apply is whether the voice is 'found within this particular writer's work and nowhere else'. For Cărtărescu I think it is. The case does not rest on fame, nationality or political symbolism. It rests on the density and architecture of the writing itself, subject to the translation caveats below.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that scale and recurring motifs (the body, the city, dream cosmology, the visionary image) may read as repetition rather than development across volumes. Carlberg and Swärd both raise this. Because I read him in translation, I cannot tell whether the original's linguistic texture justifies the length, or whether some density is an effect of translation. Carson's case is also very strong on distinctiveness and formal invention, and I ranked her second. The difference between us is narrow. It depends on whether I judge sustained quality across a whole oeuvre to be firmer in Cărtărescu's long, coherent project or in Carson's genre-crossing renewal of form.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Carson first. He argues that her voice and formal achievement are sustained across several genres and rest on deep engagement with Greek and Latin literature, so the hybrid and visual forms and the translations belong to the achievement and are not peripheral to it.
responses.response: I agree that Autobiography of Red and Nox show real invention and intellectual depth, and that antiquity gives the work substance beyond novelty. I qualify the claim that translations and scholarship are part of the literary achievement. I would anchor a citation in the original lyric, verse-novel and elegiac work and treat the translations and scholarship as context. Otherwise the citation scope blurs, and an oeuvre-wide judgment becomes harder. Our disagreement is narrow. It concerns how firmly the whole corpus holds, not whether Carson belongs among the strongest candidates, and I keep her as my first alternative.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first. He argues that the scale of the architecture is the main literary argument, closer to a constructed cosmos than to a single book. He also notes uncertainty about how much of the poetry and early work is available in translation.
responses.response: I share this reading of Cărtărescu's voice, and I accept his translation-coverage caveat as my own. The scale argument needs care, though. Size alone is not merit. The case has to rest on whether sentence-level control and imaginative invention are sustained across the long books, not on the cosmos being large. I am therefore not treating our agreement on the ranking as evidence for it. The committee should test the claim against specific passages in the original, or against the best available translations.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She credits Carson's concentrated formal inventiveness but notes that her reputation rests on a few landmark books. She also flags that Cărtărescu's later work may be repetitive in its imagery.
responses.response: Her two reservations are fair, and they are the main uncertainty in my own ranking. On the repetition point, I would separate deliberate recurrence from exhaustion. In a project built as one expanding cosmology, returning images can be structural, but I cannot verify from public knowledge that this holds in every late volume. Her point about Carson cuts the other way and deserves equal weight. If Carson's standing depends on a handful of landmark books, the sustained-quality criterion favors a writer whose whole body of work shows one developing project. That is the main reason I place Cărtărescu ahead of Carson, though I hold the judgment with moderate confidence.

responses.point: Swärd ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She finds the Romanian prose style hard to assess through translation, is less sure of the poetry and earlier prose than of the major novels, and says the recurring obsessions leave the range of the oeuvre open to debate.
responses.response: I accept the translation point, and I cannot resolve it from the supplied evidence. On range, I would say that a narrow set of obsessions does not by itself mean narrow achievement. Its limit would be real only if the books stop discovering new formal solutions. Murnane's case, which I rank third, raises the same issue in a stricter form: his method is consistent but his subject range is narrower. That is why I place Cărtărescu above Murnane, since the Romanian oeuvre spans poetry and large-scale prose across several decades. The poetry-coverage gap is a real limit on what we can claim for the whole oeuvre.

uncertainties: My assessment of Cărtărescu relies on public knowledge and translations. The stylistic density of the Romanian original is only partly accessible to me, and I cannot independently verify the translation quality of the long novels.
Translation coverage of his poetry and early prose is uncertain, so a citation naming poetry and prose together rests on less evidence for the poetry.
I cannot settle whether recurring motifs across the long novels amount to structural development or to repetition.

The comparison with Carson turns on whether sustained quality is better shown by one coherent long project or by hybrid genre-crossing invention, and on how to scope a citation for Carson's translations and scholarship. I cannot resolve this from the supplied evidence.
I have not independently read the full corpus of any shortlisted writer, and my knowledge of later and shorter works is partial.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. Documented connections are ordinary collegial ones: shared committee membership and the 2019 Academy renewal round. They do not suggest a link to any shortlisted writer. My own practice as a historical and psychological novelist is context only.
